<x_0.0322><y_0.0258>which in another part of the place may be formed on Areadian ideas; or even to be fulltituted in their feed, if they are omitted.<x_0.7402><y_0.0688><class_Text>

<x_0.0234><y_0.068>3: A part may alfo be free from either of thefe imita-tive characters, and laid out in a common limple farm, Some of the greatest beauties of nature are to be found in the fields, and attend an ordinary fate of cultiva-tion : wood and water may there be exhibited in fever-ral forms and difpoitions; we may enlarge or divide the inclofures; and give them fuch shapes and boundaries as we pleafe; every one may be an agreeable foot; together, they may compofe beautiful views; the arable, the pattern, and the mead, may succeed one another; and now and then a little wild may be intermixed with-out impropriety; every beauty, in short, which is not unusual in an included country, whether it arife from neglect or improvement, is here in its place.<x_0.7412><y_0.2625><class_Text>

<x_0.0244><y_0.2609>The buildings, alfo, which are frequent in fuch a country, are often beautiful objects; the church and the manfion are confiderable; the farm-yard itself, if an advantageous situation be chosen for it; if the ricks, and the barns, and the out-houfes, are ranged with any design to form them into groups, and if they are properly blended with trees; may be made a pictureque composition. Many of them may be detached from the groupe, and disperfed about the grounds: the dove-cote, or the diary, may be separated from the rest; they may be elegant in their forms, and placed wherever they will have the best effect. A common barn, accompanied by a clump, is fometimes placing at a distance; a Dutch barn is fo when near; and an hay-flack is generally an agreeable circumference in any potition. Each of these may be fingle; and belides thefe, all kinds of cottages are proper. Among fo many buildings, fome may be converted to other purposes than their construction denotes; and, whatever be their exterior, may within be made agreeable retreats, for refreshment, indulgence, or shelter.<x_0.7383><y_0.5484><class_Text>

<x_0.0225><y_0.5477>With fuch opportunities of improvement, even to decoration within itself, and with advantages of pro-fpect into the country about it, a limple farm may undoubtedly be delightful. It will be particularly acceptable to the owner, if it be clofe to his park or his garden; the objects which constantly remind him of his rank, impole a kind of confrontant; and he feels himself relieved, by retiring fometimes from the fplen-dor of a feat into the limplicity of a farm; it is more than a variety of feane; it is a temporary change of situation in life, which has all the charms of novelty, eafe, and tranquillity, to recommend it. A place, therefore, can hardly be deemed perfect, which is not provided with fuch a retreat. But if it be the whole of the place, it feems inadequate to the manfion: a visitor is difappointed; the matter is diffusified; he is not sufficiently diltinguished from his tenants; he miffes the appendages incidental to his feat and his fortune; and is hurt at the familiarity of his grounds with the country about them. A paltoral or an ancient farm is a little above the common level; but even thefe, if brought clofe up at the door, fet the houle in a field, where it always appears to be neglected and naked. Some degree of polith and ornament is expected in its immediate environs; and a garden, though it be but a final one, should be interpoded between the manfion and any species of farm.<x_0.7354><y_0.918><class_Text>
